bio.en: Claire Vo is a three-time chief product officer (Color, Optimizely, LaunchDarkly) and creator of ChatPRD, likely the most-used PM-specific AI product, which she builds nights and weekends.
bio.zh: Claire Vo 是三度首席产品官（Color、Optimizely、LaunchDarkly），也是 ChatPRD 的创造者——这大概是使用最广的 PM 专用 AI 产品，由她在业余时间打造。

summary.en: Claire discusses which PM skills AI will complement or replace, the story behind ChatPRD, and how to stay ahead of the curve on AI within the PM role. She emphasizes retaining agency over your career and “bending the arc” toward what you want, plus insights on being a successful woman in tech and the rise of the combined CPTO role. The conversation is rich with career advice for both early and senior product people.
summary.zh: Claire 讨论了哪些 PM 技能会被 AI 补充或替代、ChatPRD 背后的故事，以及如何在 PM 角色中保持对 AI 的领先。她强调要对职业生涯保留“主动权”并“扭转弧线”朝向自己想要的方向，以及身为科技行业成功女性、CPTO 角色崛起的洞见。对话富含对早期与资深产品人的职业建议。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: People often think that I get hired into later stage companies because I'm supposed to teach them how to operate like a big company, and in fact, I say I'm hired to remind them they can operate like a startup.
turns.zh: 人们常常认为我受聘进入后期公司是因为我应该教他们如何像大公司一样运营，事实上，我说我受聘是为了提醒他们可以像初创公司一样运营。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everybody wants this. Everyone's like, "Yes, move fast, amazing quality." What's an example of that for you?
turns.zh: 每个人都想要这个。每个人都会说，“是的，动作快，质量惊人。”您可以举个什么例子吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I communicate to my leaders that my expectation is they bring in the clock speed one click faster. If you think something needs to be done this year, it needs to be done this half.
turns.zh: 我向我的领导传达，我的期望是他们将时钟速度提高一键。如果你认为今年需要做某事，那么今年就需要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There may be a trend happening here of combining engineering product.
turns.zh: 这里可能会出现一种结合工程产品的趋势。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I'm using CPTO for short code of running product and engineering design functionally together. There should be no debates over what's best for product or what's best for engineering, what's best for design speed. What is best for the organization?
turns.zh: 我使用 CPTO 来同时运行产品和工程设计的简短代码。不应该争论什么对产品最好，什么对工程最好，什么对设计速度最好。什么对组织最有利？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You built a tool called ChatPRD. My guess is it's the single most popular AI PM-specific tool out there.
turns.zh: 您构建了一个名为 ChatPRD 的工具。我的猜测是，它是目前最流行的 AI PM 专用工具。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Is it going to eliminate PMs next year? Probably not. Are the skills required going to shift? Yes. Could they shift much faster than we all anticipate? Probably.
turns.zh: 明年会取消PM吗？可能不会。所需的技能是否会发生变化？是的。它们的转变速度会比我们预期的快得多吗？大概。

turns.zh: 这绝对是我的荣幸。 (00:04:53)：我想首先谈谈职业建议。我仔细阅读了您的 LinkedIn，您的职业道路基本上是大多数产品经理在职业生涯中所梦想的。总而言之，你从副产品经理到产品经理到高级产品经理到总监到高级总监到副总裁到高级副总裁到首席产品官，现在你已经成为三个不同公司的首席产品官。一路走来，你是创始人、设计师、工程师。 (00:05:22)：这是我的问题。如果您必须总结一下您认为在整个 PM 职业生涯中迄今为止取得如此迅速进步的秘诀是什么，那可能是什么？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, so when you list it all out, you can probably guess underneath it all is a relentlessly curious, impatient, eager to build person at their core. I just like building stuff and I find a lot of fun, and I think if you find a career or a craft that's fun, it's easy to accelerate your growth in that career. One thing, I just love what I do. (00:05:56): But when it comes to career growth and that progression from, I actually started as a copywriter of all things, copywriter all the way up to a CPO or CPTO that runs an engineering organization, it boils down to something really simple, which is know what you want out of your career, be clear and ask for it, and then make it easy for your boss or whoever can support or champion you to get you from here to there. (00:06:20): And so I'll take a really specific example from earlier in my career, where I had been in management for design and product management, so a senior manager level over product and design at an e-commerce company, and worked very closely with growth and marketing. We were just two sides of the same coin and worked very closely. And the head of marketing left and there was this big to-do pretty quickly of, "Well, what are we going to do with marketing? And do we need to hire somebody?" (00:06:49): And I sat for about a half a day and I thought, I think I can help here, drew out an org chart, put my name on the top, walked into my boss's office and said, "This is one potential solve of your marketing organization question, is we'll bring product and marketing growth together. I can be in this position. Here's how I'd change the management structure underneath this. Not just where do you put me, but where do you put everybody else? And I think this could work for the company, and this is how I'd suggest we roll it out and this would be my JD." And I got that job. I think when people ask me about career advice, they want to hear, "What can I do?" Really, what do you want? And how do you make it as easy as possible to make the case to your boss to get you here to there? (00:07:33): The other thing that I give people advice about is know what you want out of your current role and know exactly what you want your next role to be. And I even know this, and I even say this to my boss. When I was VP of product at Optimizely, I said to my boss, "I want to be a chief product officer. Here's how I'm going to get us here to there, and I want you to partner with me on it." And even coming into this role when I was interviewing at LaunchDarkly, my boss, Dan, the CEO of LaunchDarkly asked me, "What do you want out of this role?" And I said, "I want my next role to be a CEO role, so I want this role to fill in my gaps, learn, help me elevate my experience to get me to that next step." (00:08:14): And so I always know what that next role is going to be and I'm always clear about it. Now, I think there's a fine balance here. There's one thing to be very clear about your goals. It's another to suck the oxygen out of the air about only talking about getting promoted. These are probably 0.005% of my interactions with my boss are about my career growth and my path. It's very small. "Am I clear? Are we on the same page? And am I communicating as I'm making progress against those goals?" (00:08:44): High-slip people I think get promoted basically as fast as the org can support. I've almost never wished I promoted somebody earlier. I've seen managers or folks promote a little too early, and so as somebody that's managing their own career, you have to be a balance of ambitious and assertive and take care of yourself and advocate for yourself, and the work needs to speak for itself at the end of the day, and that's what's going to drive for your career growth. And so know what you want but do the work and produce the results, and you can have a career like mine.
turns.zh: 是的，所以当你把这一切都列出来时，你可能会猜到这一切的背后是一种不懈的好奇、不耐烦、渴望将人塑造为核心。我只是喜欢建造东西，并且发现了很多乐趣，而且我认为如果你找到了有趣的职业或手艺，那么很容易加速你在该职业中的成长。一件事，我只是喜欢我所做的事情。 (00:05:56)：但是说到职业发展和进步，我实际上是从一名文案撰稿人开始的，一直到运营一个工程组织的 CPO 或 CPTO，归根结底都是一些非常简单的事情，那就是知道你想从你的职业生涯中得到什么，明确并要求它，然后让你的老板或任何可以支持或支持你的人轻松地让你从这里到那里。 (00:06:20)：我将举一个我职业生涯早期的具体例子，我曾在一家电子商务公司从事设计和产品管理工作，担任产品和设计方面的高级经理，并与增长和营销部门密切合作。我们只是同一枚硬币的两面，而且合作非常密切。营销主管离开了，很快就有了一件大事要做，“好吧，我们要在营销方面做什么？我们需要雇人吗？” (00:06:49)：我坐了大约半天，我想，我想我可以在这里帮忙，画了一张组织结构图，把我的名字写在上面，走进老板的办公室说，“这是营销组织问题的一个潜在解决方案，我们将把产品和营销增长结合在一起。我可以处于这个位置。这就是我如何改变管理结构的方法。不仅仅是你把我放在哪里，还有你把其他人放在哪里？然后我认为这对公司有用，这就是我建议我们推出它的方式，这将是我的 JD。”我得到了那份工作。我认为当人们向我询问职业建议时，他们想听的是“我能做什么？”真的，你想要什么？如何才能尽可能轻松地向老板提出让你到达那里的理由？ (00:07:33)：我给人们的建议的另一件事是知道你想从当前的角色中得到什么，并确切地知道你想要的下一个角色是什么。我什至知道这一点，我什至对我的老板也这么说。当我在 Optimizely 担任产品副总裁时，我对老板说：“我想成为一名首席产品官。这就是我将如何让我们从这里到那里，我希望你能与我合作。”甚至当我在 LaunchDarkly 面试时，我的老板、LaunchDarkly 的首席执行官 Dan 就问我：“你想从这个职位中得到什么？”我说，“我希望我的下一个角色是首席执行官，所以我希望这个角色能够填补我的空白，学习，帮助我提升我的经验，让我迈出下一步。” (00:08:14)：所以我总是知道下一个角色将会是什么，而且我总是很清楚。现在，我认为这里有一个很好的平衡。有一点需要非常清楚你的目标。只谈论升职而吸走空气中的氧气是另一回事。在我与老板的互动中，大概有 0.005% 是关于我的职业发展和我的道路的。它非常小。 “我说清楚了吗？我们意见一致吗？当我在实现这些目标方面取得进展时，我是否进行了沟通？” (00:08:44)：我认为高滑率的人基本上会按照组织能够支持的速度得到晋升。我几乎从来不希望自己能够更早地提拔某人。我见过经理或员工晋升得太早了，所以作为管理自己职业生涯的人，你必须在雄心勃勃和自信之间取得平衡，照顾好自己并为自己辩护，工作需要在一天结束时不言自明，这才是推动你职业发展的动力。因此，知道自己想要什么，但付出努力并取得成果，你就可以拥有像我这样的职业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe first to summarize, some of the core advice you're sharing is know what you actually want because you're not going to progress towards this amazing future career if you don't actually know where you're going. Otherwise, you'll be pushed in directions that you're not necessarily interested in going. (00:09:38): I have a sense of where you want to go to tell people and ask for it. "Here's what I want to be doing in the future. Help me get there." And I love the other point you made of just, don't over-focus on that. There's many people that spend a lot of their energy on, "I need to get promoted. How do I get to the next level? I deserve the next level." And I guess maybe along those lines, is there any other advice you could share of just how to avoid being that person that's just constantly obsessed with promotion? Any more advice of just how to find that balance?
turns.zh: 也许首先要总结一下，您分享的一些核心建议是知道您真正想要什么，因为如果您实际上不知道自己要去哪里，您就不会朝着这个令人惊叹的未来职业发展。否则，你会被推向你不一定感兴趣的方向。 (00:09:38)：我知道你想去哪里告诉人们并要求它。 “这就是我将来想做的事情。帮助我实现目标。”我喜欢你提出的另一点，不要过度关注这一点。有很多人花了很多精力在“我需要晋升。我如何才能升到下一个级别？我值得升到下一个级别”。我想也许沿着这些思路，你还有什么其他建议可以分享，如何避免成为那个不断沉迷于晋升的人？关于如何找到这种平衡还有更多建议吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah. One, you've got to lock to the norms, the talent norms of your organization. You should know how those things work, and they can work very casually if you're a very small startup and they can work more formally if you're at a very large company. And one, understanding how promotions operationally happen inside an organization can help you have those conversations at the right time in the right moment with the right context. That's one thing I advise. We're a slightly larger organization. We do promotion cycles. We have times during which we promote people. And so if you're talking to me four months before a promo cycle, maybe it's top of mind, maybe it's not. I sometimes functionally cannot promote people inside larger organizations whenever I want. (00:10:52): One is, I think, understanding the talent calendar of your team, especially at a larger organization. I think the second thing is really the conversation needs to be about what you being in a different position does for the company and why the company needs it. Often the conversation is, "I want to be promoted because I want to be a director of PM, because I want to become a manager, because I need direct reports." Instead of saying, "Look, your span of control, you have nine direct reports, you need leverage here. I have a lot of credibility with this side of the product organization. I think we could be doing more if this position existed. And I think I'm good for this position because of what I've proven A, B and C." (00:11:43): That's solving a problem for the company. That's not solving a career growth issue for an individual. And I think people who want to be promoted need to think in that orientation versus the other, because honestly, especially now, let's say [inaudible 00:12:01]. There are not just these wrote every 12 months we're going to give comp increases and merit increases and you get to be promoted. We really have to be thoughtful about the structure and size and organization of teams. Product teams are naturally pretty small. (00:12:19): So, there aren't just management and director and senior director roles to go around. And if you want to get into a management, for example, you have to prove that you're good at organization design. I think really focus on why a role is good for a company or necessary for a company and then why you are the best for that role, rather than, "I want to get promoted."
turns.zh: 是的。第一，你必须遵守组织的规范，即人才规范。你应该知道这些东西是如何工作的，如果你是一家非常小的初创公司，它们可以非常随意地工作；如果你在一家非常大的公司，它们可以更正式地工作。第一，了解组织内部促销活动的运作方式可以帮助您在正确的时间、正确的背景下进行这些对话。这是我建议的一件事。我们是一个规模稍大的组织。我们进行促销周期。我们有时会提拔员工。因此，如果您在促销周期前四个月与我交谈，也许这是首要考虑的事情，也许不是。有时，我在职能上无法随时提拔大型组织内的人员。 (00:10:52)：我认为，一是了解团队的人才日历，尤其是在较大的组织中。我认为第二件事实际上是对话需要讨论你处于不同的职位对公司有何作用以及公司为什么需要它。通常的对话是，“我想升职，因为我想成为 PM 总监，因为我想成为经理，因为我需要直接报告。”而不是说，“看，你的控制范围，你有九个直接报告，你需要在这里发挥影响力。我对产品组织的这一方面有很大的可信度。我认为如果这个职位存在，我们可以做得更多。而且我认为我很适合这个职位，因为我已经证明了 A、B 和 C。” (00:11:43)：这为公司解决了问题。这并不能解决个人的职业发展问题。我认为想要晋升的人需要从这个方向思考，而不是从另一个方向思考，因为说实话，尤其是现在，让我们说 [听不清 00:12:01]。不仅仅是每 12 个月写的这些，我们还会提高薪酬和绩效，然后你就会得到晋升。我们确实必须考虑团队的结构、规模和组织。产品团队自然很小。 (00:12:19)：因此，不仅仅有管理、总监和高级总监的角色。例如，如果你想进入管理层，你必须证明你擅长组织设计。我认为真正关注的是为什么某个职位对公司有利或对公司来说是必要的，然后为什么你最适合这个职位，而不是“我想升职”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such good advice and such important advice that focus on how do you solve problems for your manager and the business, not, "Hey, here's what I need for my career. This sucks. My career is stagnating." I love that. And I love so much of your message is empowerment. It's not just, here, there's the place you're in and there's not a lot you can do about it. Look for opportunities to help your manager, help your business. "Here's what I can do to move things further." (00:13:06): And I think there's an element of timing that you touched on. Propose this at a time when something could happen. You shared this example of there was a marketing gap.
turns.zh: 这是很好的建议，也是很重要的建议，重点是如何为经理和企业解决问题，而不是“嘿，这就是我职业生涯所需的东西。这很糟糕。我的职业生涯停滞不前。”我喜欢那个。我非常喜欢你传达的信息：赋权。不仅仅是，在这里，在你所处的地方，你对此无能为力。寻找机会帮助你的经理，帮助你的企业。 “我可以采取以下措施来推动事情进一步发展。” (00:13:06)：我认为您提到了时间因素。在可能发生事情的时候提出这个建议。您分享了这个存在营销差距的例子。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yep, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there another example where you did this sort of thing where you presented, "Here's how I can help the org," and that helped another promotion? If not, that's good.
turns.zh: 是否还有另一个例子，您做了这样的事情，您提出“我可以如何帮助该组织”，这有助于另一次晋升？如果没有，那很好。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: It's honestly how I expanded into leading engineering teams in the technology organization. I was at Color and there was a real need to up-level our engineering organization, and I knew exactly what to do. I had high confidence I had the skills, both technical and organizational, to scale the engineering organization in a way that was really critical to the business, both from a architecture perspective and from a team and talent perspective. And so that was one where I knew there was a problem to solve. I knew that problem was important. I knew we had to solve it fast, and I was confident I knew I could do it. I had confidence that I could help there. (00:14:06): And so I'm still doing it today. And at Color, I came in as product. I very quickly began leading the engineering organization, which was fabulous, and then I actually took on some of our non-clinical operations as well where we had a pretty operational leader. We had some high-scale challenges to deal with, and it fit my talent set and I knew I could help the company pretty quickly. (00:14:32): And this is the other advice I might give particular to PMs. PM is such a generalist role, it's okay to go a little left and a little right to go up. I took this marketing growth role. That was actually my first director role. It wasn't only for product, it was for marketing. And I had to learn marketing and I had to develop skills there, but it was a foundation on which I could build a broader leadership career. And so I do think also looking left and right outside of your scope of product can be a really effective way to find growth opportunities.
turns.zh: 老实说，这就是我如何扩展到技术组织中领先的工程团队的。我在 Color 工作，确实需要提升我们的工程组织水平，而且我确切地知道该怎么做。我非常有信心自己拥有技术和组织方面的技能，能够以对业务真正至关重要的方式扩展工程组织，无论是从架构角度还是从团队和人才角度来看。所以这就是我知道有一个问题需要解决的地方。我知道这个问题很重要。我知道我们必须快速解决这个问题，而且我相信我可以做到。我有信心我可以在那里提供帮助。 (00:14:06)：所以我今天仍在这样做。在 Color，我是作为产品加入的。我很快就开始领导工程组织，这非常棒，然后我实际上还承担了一些非临床业务，我们有一位相当出色的运营领导者。我们需要应对一些大规模的挑战，这符合我的才能，而且我知道我可以很快帮助公司。 (00:14:32)：这是我可能特别向产品经理提出的另一个建议。 PM就是这么一个多面手的角色，往左走一点，往右走一点就可以了。我担任了营销增长的角色。这实际上是我的第一个导演角色。这不仅是为了产品，也是为了营销。我必须学习营销，必须在那里发展技能，但这是我可以建立更广泛的领导职业生涯的基础。因此，我确实认为，在产品范围之外左右寻找可能是寻找增长机会的真正有效方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice, and it leads to so many unexpected opportunities. One of the, I think, big questions with PMs, and coming back to your original advice of know where you want to go, there's so many directions a PM can go. You can eventually become a founder, become a GM, become a CO, something else. And trying these sorts of things often helps you understand, "Here's what I'm actually excited about. Maybe I want to move into design."
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个建议，它会带来很多意想不到的机会。我认为，PM 面临的一个大问题是，回到你最初的建议，知道你想去哪里，PM 可以走很多方向。你最终可以成为创始人、总经理、首席运营官或其他职位。尝试这些事情通常可以帮助你理解，“这就是我真正兴奋的事情。也许我想进入设计领域。”

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, and one of the other things that I think people don't understand, and maybe I experienced this as a founder and I really feel it inside companies, is the universe is bendable to your will. And what I mean is in most, at least in the stage I operate in in startups and growth stage companies and late stage startups, organizations are very fluid and I like to organize around talented motivated individuals. (00:15:58): And so just because we're organized in a particular way now, just because these organizations are separate or these are different, together, doesn't mean that's necessarily the way they have to be, and so you should think about your career growth in the existing structure of the organization. But as an org design thinker, it's a very important job that I have to do. You also have to think of this system as a living, breathing entity that can shift over time in particular around highly motivated, highly talented people.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为人们不理解的另一件事是，宇宙是可以屈服于你的意志的，也许我作为创始人经历过这一点，我在公司内部也确实感受到了这一点。我的意思是，在大多数情况下，至少在我所处的初创公司、成长期公司和后期初创公司运营的阶段，组织非常流动，我喜欢围绕有才华、积极进取的个人进行组织。 (00:15:58)：所以仅仅因为我们现在以特定的方式组织，仅仅因为这些组织是独立的或不同的，但并不意味着它们一定是这样的，所以你应该在组织的现有结构中考虑你的职业发展。但作为一名组织设计思想家，这是我必须做的一项非常重要的工作。你还必须将这个系统视为一个活生生的、会呼吸的实体，它可以随着时间的推移而发生变化，特别是在积极性高、才华横溢的人周围。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think along the same lines, referencing this advice you've already shared of just thinking from the perspective of what is my manager and folks above, what are they struggling with and how can I propose, "Here's a solution that happens to also have me move into a more interesting role?"
turns.zh: 我认为沿着同样的思路，参考你已经分享的这个建议，只是从我的经理和上面的人的角度思考，他们正在挣扎什么，我该如何提出，“这是一个解决方案，碰巧也让我进入一个更有趣的角色？”

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yep, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a direction I wasn't planning to go into, but I think it's really important and interesting is people like you that are incredibly good and successful end up taking on a lot, and that often ends up not being what they want.
turns.zh: 有一个我原本没有打算进入的方向，但我认为非常重要和有趣的是像你这样非常优秀和成功的人最终承担了很多，而这往往不是他们想要的。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: SOS.
turns.zh: 求救。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly. Any advice on the classic, be careful what you're good at advice? Any advice on just how to not end up with everything?
turns.zh: 确切地。对经典有什么建议吗，小心你擅长的建议吗？关于如何避免一切都结束有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I really believe operating in your zone of genius. I really believe in leaning into strengths. And if you are in a position in which you're good at things and you've been giving a lot of responsibility, but you have tremendous growth edges and you're spending more time on the things you need to level up than the things you are exceptional at, I think that's not fair for the organization. I think that's not fair for you. (00:17:32): I truly believe defining and understanding your zone of genius, where you are exceptional, where no one else can step into the job and do just as good of a job as you can, and where you derive tremendous intellectual emotional joy out of the work is what makes it sustainable over time. And so I don't actually think it's about the volume or breadth of the work. It's about sustainability of the work. And can you show up every day energized and engaged and excited about what you do? (00:18:04): And I think being very aware if you are operating the space or if you're not. And this might go back to, I think, I have never regretted promoting somebody too slowly, I have regretted promoting somebody too quickly. High-slope individuals in particular areas want to get more responsibility, want to have more scope, and I've seen less experienced managers or directors or even people at my level want to give opportunities that put people in a position where they're neither effective nor happy. And so I think being self-aware of that is really important, and then I also think as a manager, being cognizant of that is really important. (00:18:50): Individually, I do do a lot, but I do feel like I'm in my zone of genius and I also know that part of staying in my personal zone of genius is having this breadth of responsibility but preserving builder time. And what I mean from time is I have to have time to produce real work that comes from me as an individual, and that means that calendar management is quite important. Time management.
turns.zh: 我真的相信在你的天才区域里工作。我真的相信要发挥优势。如果你处于一个擅长做事并且承担了很多责任的职位，但你有巨大的成长优势，你花在需要提升的事情上的时间比你擅长的事情上的时间多，我认为这对组织来说是不公平的。我认为这对你不公平。 (00:17:32)：我坚信定义和理解你的天才区，你是杰出的，没有其他人可以进入工作并像你一样出色地完成工作，并且你从工作中获得巨大的智力情感快乐，这使得它能够随着时间的推移而可持续。所以我实际上并不认为这与工作的数量或广度有关。这是关于工作的可持续性。你能每天都对自己所做的事情充满活力、投入和兴奋吗？ (00:18:04)：我认为要非常清楚您是否正在操作该空间。我想，这可能会追溯到，我从来没有后悔提拔某人太慢，我后悔提拔某人太快。特定领域的高坡度个人想要获得更多责任，想要拥有更大的范围，我见过经验不足的经理或董事，甚至像我这样级别的人想要提供机会，让人们处于既不高效也不快乐的境地。所以我认为自我意识非常重要，而且我也认为作为一名经理，认识到这一点非常重要。 (00:18:50)：就个人而言，我确实做了很多事情，但我确实觉得自己处于我的天才区域，而且我也知道保持在我个人天才区域的一部分是承担如此广泛的责任，但保留建设者的时间。我的意思是，我必须有时间来完成我个人的实际工作，这意味着日历管理非常重要。时间管理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to talk about some of the things that you built. (00:19:23): In terms of finding your zone of genius, any advice for someone that's trying to figure out what it is that is in that zone of genius? I know there's a Ted Talk of here's how to think about the zone of genius specifically [inaudible 00:19:33].
turns.zh: 我们将讨论您构建的一些东西。 (00:19:23)：在寻找你的天才区方面，对于那些试图弄清楚天才区是什么的人有什么建议吗？我知道有一个 Ted 演讲，讨论了如何具体思考天才区域 [听不清 00:19:33]。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah. I'm not going to relay it in precision, but one of the tactics that I've seen out there is basically go through your calendar for the last month or quarter, whatever it is, write everything down, and basically group them into, I hated doing this, I didn't love doing it but it was fine, I love doing this, and then I love doing this, and if I could spend all my time on this, I would be the happiest person in the whole world. And literally categorize the way you're spending your time into those buckets, and then put the bottom buckets away. Just focus on that top bucket and go, "How can I be here more?" And often, that is a true guide to where your passion is, where your special expertise is, and where you're going to add a lot of value because you're highly engaged. (00:20:26): I think the other thing is really asking yourself, and this maybe goes back to the career advice perspective, really asking yourself, "What do I do that no one else in this organization can do?" There are lots of things that I do that other people in the organization can do, but what are the things that I do that are... You think about a differentiated product that are hard to replicate, and knowing what that is and leaning into that can drive a lot of exceptional career growth but also just make you quite happy.
turns.zh: 是的。我不会精确地转达它，但我看到的策略之一基本上是浏览上个月或上个季度的日历，无论是什么，把所有内容都写下来，然后将它们基本上分组为，我讨厌这样做，我不喜欢这样做，但没关系，我喜欢这样做，然后我喜欢这样做，如果我能把所有的时间都花在这上面，我将是世界上最幸福的人。从字面上将你花费时间的方式分类到这些桶中，然后把最底层的桶收起来。只需专注于最上面的桶并思考“我怎样才能在这里更多？”通常，这是一个真正的指南，告诉你你的热情在哪里，你的特殊专长在哪里，以及你将在哪里增加很多价值，因为你高度投入。 (00:20:26)：我认为另一件事是真正问自己，这也许可以回到职业建议的角度，真正问自己，“我能做什么，这个组织中没有其他人可以做？”我做的很多事情是组织中的其他人可以做的，但我所做的事情是……你会想到一种难以复制的差异化产品，了解它是什么并倾向于它可以推动许多非凡的职业发展，同时也让你感到非常高兴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that for you?
turns.zh: 您可以举个什么例子吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I think I'm actually quite good at traversing across and up and down. What I mean is I am fluent across product engineering, design, data and operations, and candidly revenue in a way that vertical or functional leaders maybe are less so. I feel like I have a high level of fluency broadly and can bring conversations between functions together against a business objective pretty easily. It's just the way I'm wired. I was a founder. It's second nature. (00:21:31): And the other thing that I think I can do pretty well that I find very joyous is traverse elevation. And so, yes, I love to be up here and think about strategy and vision, but I also like to drop into the details to move things forward. And I think that operating horizontally and then being able to spend some time in the vertical up and down, wherever that vertical up and down happens makes me quite happy. I think I'm pretty good at it.
turns.zh: 我想我其实很擅长穿越、上下穿越。我的意思是，我对产品工程、设计、数据和运营以及坦率的收入都很熟悉，而垂直或职能领导者可能不那么擅长。我觉得我在很大程度上具有很高的流畅性，并且可以很容易地将职能之间的对话结合起来以实现业务目标。这就是我的接线方式。我是一名创始人。这是第二天性。 (00:21:31)：另一件我认为我可以做得很好并且让我感到非常高兴的事情是横向海拔。所以，是的，我喜欢在这里思考战略和愿景，但我也喜欢深入细节以推动事情向前发展。我认为，水平操作，然后能够花一些时间在垂直向上和向下，无论垂直向上和向下发生的地方，都让我非常高兴。我认为我很擅长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We're going to touch on some of these things you just mentioned actually, but real quick, you mentioned this idea of essentially an energy audit. There's actually a really good guide that I'll point to in the show notes by Matt Mochary that walks you through how to do this. And we talk about this a bunch on this podcast actually, this whole idea of just find things that give you energy, do more of that. Find things that zap you of energy, do less of that. Easier said than done when you have a job and you have to do stuff that people are paying you to do, but it's still really helpful if nothing else to help you point you where you want to be going in your career long-term. (00:22:29): Okay, so you mentioned you're a founder, and it feels like you're a founder at heart, but you've been working at larger companies for a while now. And I hear that you're really good at setting a fast pace within larger companies and maintaining that startup focus while also having a very high bar for quality and product. Everybody wants this. Everyone's like, "Yes, move fast, amazing quality." Why would we not want that? I'm curious just what you actually put into practice concretely that allow for you to build teams that move really fast and maintain a high bar. Are there processes you find helpful, values, ways of working?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我们将讨论您刚才提到的一些事情，但很快，您提到了能源审计的想法。实际上，我将在 Matt Mochary 的演出笔记中指出一个非常好的指南，它会引导您完成此操作。事实上，我们在这个播客上讨论了很多这个问题，就是找到能给你能量的东西，做更多的事情。寻找那些消耗你能量的事情，少做一些。当你有一份工作，而且你必须做人们付钱给你做的事情时，说起来容易做起来难，但如果没有其他办法可以帮助你指明你想要在职业生涯中长期发展的方向，它仍然非常有帮助。 (00:22:29)：好的，你提到你是一名创始人，感觉你本质上就是一名创始人，但你已经在大公司工作了一段时间了。我听说您非常擅长在大公司中设定快速节奏并保持初创公司的重点，同时对质量和产品也有很高的标准。每个人都想要这个。每个人都会说，“是的，动作快，质量惊人。”为什么我们不想要这样呢？我很好奇你实际上具体付诸了哪些实践，让你能够建立行动迅速并保持高标准的团队。您认为哪些流程、价值观和工作方式对您有帮助？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, it's really funny, people often think that I get hired into the roles that I get hired into in later stage companies because I'm supposed to teach them how to operate like a big company. And in fact, I say I'm hired to remind them they can operate like a startup. And so I think about it completely differently. (00:23:23): And there are two things I think about in terms of pace and high bar. From a pace, it's know what your internal pace is, and essentially don't let it degrade to the pace of your recurring meetings. I often find that pace of organization locks to pace of the calendar, and so I am really thoughtful that reoccurring meetings do not drive next steps. It's a very tactical thing, but when somebody says, "Oh, we'll discuss this or we'll decide this in the next meeting," it's, "No, we should discuss this now. We should decide this tomorrow." (00:23:58): The other thing that I think about is setting one click faster pace expectations inside an organization. I tend to come in and love this, hate it, it's what I do, which is if I look at an organization that is operating at a lower pace than I would expect, I communicate to my leaders that my expectation is they bring in the clock speed one click faster, which means if you think something needs to be done this year, it needs to be done this half. If you think it needs to be done this half, it needs to be done this quarter. This quarter, this month. This week, today. End of day, in this meeting. And actually setting an expectation that your natural pace is going to be slower than your ambition and being explicit about pulling things in I think can change the way expectations are set and honestly change the energy and momentum in the organization. (00:24:51): The third thing on pace is personal SLA. I never want to be a bottleneck for the organization. This is one of the more challenging things about being in my role, is you are often a point of decision-making, tie-breaking, next steps, approvals, socialization. And if my personal SLA is slow, then the rest of my organization cannot be as fast as possible. I try to be fairly responsive. I try to say, "Do both very high rate," and also very quickly. It's really hard, sometimes it's not totally possible, but it's a goal I have.
turns.zh: 是的，这真的很有趣，人们经常认为我被雇用到我在后期公司中被雇用的角色，因为我应该教他们如何像大公司一样运作。事实上，我说我被雇佣是为了提醒他们他们可以像初创公司一样运作。所以我的想法完全不同。 (00:23:23)：关于速度和高标准，我考虑了两件事。从节奏上看，它知道您的内部节奏是什么，并且本质上不要让它降低到您定期会议的节奏。我经常发现组织的节奏与日历的节奏锁定，所以我真的很想，重复召开的会议不会推动后续步骤。这是一个非常战术性的事情，但是当有人说，“哦，我们将讨论这个问题，或者我们将在下次会议上决定这个问题”时，“不，我们应该现在讨论这个问题。我们应该明天就决定这个问题。” (00:23:58)：我想到的另一件事是在组织内部设定一键更快的速度期望。我倾向于喜欢这个，讨厌它，这就是我所做的，如果我看到一个组织的运营速度低于我的预期，我会向我的领导者传达我的期望是他们将时钟速度加快一键，这意味着如果你认为今年需要做某件事，那么就需要在今年完成。如果你认为这半年需要完成，那么这个季度就需要完成。这个季度，这个月。这周，今天。今天的会议结束了。实际上设定一个期望，即你的自然节奏将慢于你的野心，并明确地把事情拉进去，我认为可以改变期望的设定方式，并诚实地改变组织的能量和动力。 (00:24:51)：节奏上的第三件事是个人 SLA。我从来不想成为组织的瓶颈。这是担任我的角色时更具挑战性的事情之一，因为你经常是决策、打破平局、下一步、批准、社交的关键。如果我个人的 SLA 很慢，那么我组织的其他部分就无法尽可能快。我尽量做出适当的回应。我试着说，“两者都做到非常高的速度”，而且速度非常快。这真的很难，有时并不完全可能，但这是我的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this clock speed concept of just let's move one iteration faster than we would normally move. How do you actually do that? Is this just you doing it and then everyone trickles down from the way you're approaching it? Is this a principle on a team? Is there a phrase you use?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种时钟速度概念，即让我们比正常情况下更快地移动一次迭代。你实际上是如何做到的？难道只有你在这样做，然后每个人都从你的做法中吸取教训吗？这是团队的原则吗？有你使用的短语吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, it's a phrase I use and something I asked our leadership teams to do. It started at, one, I'm going to do this, and two, my expectation is you look for opportunities to do this. And the reason I think this is effective, it's very tangible and it's very tactical. It just is one of those things that a moment when you're about to say a due date, you check yourself and you go, "Is this right or do I need to pull it in by an iteration?" And so it's a very tactical piece of advice and expectation I give to my leadership team. If they can show up that way, then the expected pace of the organization goes up, and then people tend to rise to the occasion.
turns.zh: 是的，这是我使用的一个短语，也是我要求我们的领导团队做的事情。一开始，我要这样做，第二，我的期望是你寻找机会这样做。我认为这是有效的，因为它非常有形，而且非常有策略性。这只是其中一件事，当你即将说出截止日期时，你会检查自己，然后问：“这是正确的还是我需要通过迭代来拉动它？”所以这是我给我的领导团队的一个非常战术性的建议和期望。如果他们能够以这种方式出现，那么组织的预期步伐就会加快，然后人们就会倾向于应对这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then it connects very directly to your first piece of advice, is not rely on the meeting cadence to determine your action cadence. I imagine that's a similar situation where you tell people, "Here's how I want to operate," and then you actually work that way and that starts to filter through.
turns.zh: 然后它与你的第一条建议非常直接地联系在一起，不是依靠会议节奏来决定你的行动节奏。我想这是一个类似的情况，你告诉人们，“这就是我想要的运作方式”，然后你实际上就按照这种方式工作，并且开始渗透进来。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, I just think there's this anti-pattern of, "We'll make the decision in the next meeting," or, "We'll follow up on this in the next meeting." That is an artificial timeline introduced by Google Calendar or whatever calendar you use. It's not a real thing, and so I want to put us on real timelines. When can we make the decision? How much information do we need? And that doesn't mean that every decision is made now, today, tomorrow, but it does mean we don't snap to artificial cadences to make our product move forward.
turns.zh: 是的，我只是认为存在这种反模式，“我们将在下次会议上做出决定”，或者“我们将在下次会议上跟进此事”。这是由 Google 日历或您使用的任何日历引入的人工时间线。这不是真实的事情，所以我想让我们了解真实的时间表。我们什么时候可以做出决定？我们需要多少信息？这并不意味着每一个决定都是现在、今天、明天做出的，但这确实意味着我们不会为了让我们的产品向前发展而遵循人为的节奏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Let's talk about quality. What are some lessons there?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我们来谈谈质量。那里有什么教训？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, I think in terms of high bar, there's probably two things that I think about as a leader. There's the talent bar being exceptionally high, and then there's the product bar being high. (00:27:28): I'll start with talent, which is, on the talent side I think you have to define the bar. You have to be really specific, and that means you have to think about pretty deeply what are your leadership principles? If your leadership principle is bring the clock speed up one iteration, be explicit that that's what you expect to see, and then articulate that and hold people accountable to it. (00:27:51): And so I do think it's really important to have a specific and measurable career ladder, especially at the senior levels. I often find that they're very soft. They're hires and manages multiple departments or takes in cross-functional stakeholder feedback. Those are just not tractable, specific things. And so I think, PMs, put on your product definition or OKR hat or whatever and define some real goals for these levels and be specific in a way that you can look at people and say, definitively, "Yes. Measurably, yes, they're meaning this bar measurably. No, they're not meeting that bar." And so I think that's very important. (00:28:39): The second thing I think is you have to normalize feedback. And Brené Brown, fellow Texan, love her, "Clear is kind," I think conflict-avoidant, feedback-avoidant cultures degrade the talent bar. They just do, because the expectations are not stated and you're not holding accountability. And I do not think that's kind. That is not setting up people for success in their careers. That is not helping them become the best teammate that they can become. (00:29:08): I really like to normalize feedback and, as I say, take the temperature out of the room when it comes to open and candid feedback. And that means being very clear when people are not meeting expectations, making it very clear that questioning ideas is not questioning innate talent. And I think that has something that people need to hear to normalize feedback. But I think feedback is quite important. (00:29:30): And I think the third thing is unfortunately when you're working to build a high talent bar and high talent density, then when folks aren't a fit and it's not working, moving against that quickly is part of the job. And it's a hard part of the job and it's part of the job that most managers really avoid, but I think it's important because it keeps your overall team operating in a really healthy, effective, performant way that makes everybody happier, including people that probably weren't a great fit for the work of the role at the time.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为就高标准而言，作为领导者我可能会考虑两件事。人才门槛非常高，产品门槛也很高。 (00:27:28)：我将从人才开始，也就是说，在人才方面，我认为你必须定义标准。你必须非常具体，这意味着你必须深入思考你的领导原则是什么？如果你的领导原则是加快一次迭代的速度，请明确表明这是你期望看到的，然后阐明这一点并让人们对此负责。 (00:27:51)：所以我确实认为拥有一个具体且可衡量的职业阶梯非常重要，尤其是在高层。我经常发现它们非常柔软。他们雇用和管理多个部门，或接受跨职能利益相关者的反馈。这些只是难以处理的具体事情。所以我认为，产品经理们，戴上你的产品定义或 OKR 帽子或其他什么，为这些级别定义一些真正的目标，并以一种具体的方式，你可以看着人们并明确地说，“是的。可衡量的，是的，他们是可衡量的这个标准。不，他们没有达到那个标准。”所以我认为这非常重要。 (00:28:39)：我认为第二件事是你必须规范反馈。德克萨斯同胞布蕾妮·布朗 (Brené Brown) 很喜欢她，“清晰就是善良”，我认为回避冲突、回避反馈的文化降低了人才标准。他们只是这么做，因为没有明确说明期望，而且你也不承担责任。我认为这并不友善。这并不能帮助人们取得职业成功。这并不能帮助他们成为最好的队友。 (00:29:08)：我真的很喜欢将反馈标准化，正如我所说，在公开和坦诚的反馈方面，要消除房间里的温度。这意味着当人们没有达到期望时要非常清楚，明确质疑想法并不是质疑天赋。我认为人们需要听到一些东西才能使反馈正常化。但我认为反馈非常重要。 (00:29:30)：我认为第三件事是不幸的是，当你努力建立一个高人才标准和高人才密度时，当人们不适合并且不起作用时，快速采取行动就是工作的一部分。这是工作中困难的一部分，也是大多数经理真正回避的工作的一部分，但我认为这很重要，因为它使整个团队以真正健康、有效、高效的方式运作，让每个人都更快乐，包括那些可能不太适合当时该职位工作的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of you being surprisingly candid to someone or giving feedback, hard feedback, to someone about quality, something that's just like, "Oh wow, that's what I should be doing?"
turns.zh: 有没有一个例子表明你对某人出奇的坦诚，或者向某人提供有关质量的反馈，严厉的反馈，就像“哦哇，这就是我应该做的？”

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: There were two leaders in my organization, I won't say which ones and I won't say when, but two leaders in the organization, partners across product and engineering, and they could not get it together. They could not work together. They were having misalignments and priorities strategy. They could not communicate. They were having conflict in front of the team. (00:30:38): And the managers that had managed them were taking this very soft pedal approach of, "You need to work on your [inaudible 00:30:47] functional stakeholder, and here am I expecting all this performance management stuff to happen." And I called both of them individually and I said, "The way you are operating is not meeting our leadership expectations. If you do not change, you cannot be part of this organization anymore. I believe you can operate differently. I do." And I did. I believe these are very talented people who could operate. "I believe you can operate differently, but it is your responsibility to do so, and I need to see change starting tomorrow." (00:31:20): I wanted them to succeed. And in fact, they did. It snapped in, they got it, and one of the... Turned into one of the most influential effective managers in our team over the course of probably the next six to nine months. And I think just clearly saying, "You are not meeting expectations. You will not be successful here if you continue on this path. I believe you can get here, but it is your responsibility." That is the conversation that is clear and kind and honestly very effective in most instances.
turns.zh: 我的组织中有两位领导者，我不会说是哪一位，也不会说何时，但是组织中有两位领导者，跨产品和工程的合作伙伴，但他们无法团结在一起。他们无法一起工作。他们的战略和优先事项不一致。他们无法沟通。他们在团队面前发生了冲突。 (00:30:38)：管理它们的管理者正在采取这种非常温和的方法，“你需要为你的[听不清的00:30:47]职能利益相关者工作，我期待所有这些绩效管理的事情都会发生。”我分别给他们俩打电话，说：“你们的运作方式没有达到我们领导层的期望。如果你们不改变，你们就不能再成为这个组织的一部分。我相信你们可以采取不同的运作方式。我相信。”我做到了。我相信这些都是非常有才华的人，可以操作。 “我相信你可以采取不同的运作方式，但这样做是你的责任，我需要从明天开始看到改变。” (00:31:20)：我希望他们成功。事实上，他们确实做到了。他们突然明白了，他们明白了，其中一位……在接下来的六到九个月的时间里，变成了我们团队中最有影响力的高效经理之一。我认为只是明确地说，“你没有达到期望。如果你继续走这条路，你不会在这里成功。我相信你可以到达这里，但这是你的责任。”在大多数情况下，这种对话是清晰、友善且诚实且非常有效的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing example. Clear is kind, as you said. It reminds me of Kim Scott, who's on the podcast, shared this story about Bob. I don't know if you remember that story at all of just this guy at their company who was just doing a bad job and everyone knew he was doing a bad job, and then they had to fire him. When they're firing him, he's just like, "Why didn't you tell me? Why didn't anyone tell me that nobody thought I was doing a great job?"
turns.zh: 这是一个了不起的例子。正如你所说，清晰是善良的。这让我想起播客上的金·斯科特分享了这个关于鲍勃的故事。我不知道你是否还记得他们公司里这个人的故事，他工作做得很糟糕，每个人都知道他做得很糟糕，然后他们不得不解雇他。当他们解雇他时，他只是说，“你为什么不告诉我？为什么没有人告诉我，没有人认为我做得很好？”

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: And I honestly think saying, "You are not doing a good job," is much kinder than, "I think you can improve on this aspect or that aspect." Or, "I've gotten some feedback that you could be better at..." That's not kind because it doesn't set somebody else up for success either in your organization or somewhere else.
turns.zh: 老实说，我认为说“你做得不好”比说“我认为你可以在这个或那个方面改进”要友善得多。或者，“我收到了一些反馈，认为你可以做得更好……”这并不友善，因为它不会让其他人在你的组织或其他地方取得成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's go in a different direction. Let's talk about being a woman in tech.
turns.zh: 好吧，我们换个方向吧。让我们来谈谈如何成为一名科技界的女性。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This doesn't get talked about a ton on podcasts like this. I know you have a lot of thoughts. Obviously, you've been through a lot. You've had a lot of experiences. There's probably a lot of stories you haven't shared in other places, so I just want to give you a chance to share what you've been through, what you've seen, and any advice you may have.
turns.zh: 在这样的播客上，这一点并没有得到太多讨论。我知道你有很多想法。显然，你经历了很多。你已经有很多经历了。可能有很多故事你没有在其他地方分享过，所以我只是想给你一个机会来分享你所经历的、你所看到的、以及你可能有的建议。

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: Yeah, and I'm happy to talk about this. I know a lot of people don't want to be defined or consistently asked about being a woman or a mom in a C-level leadership role. Let's not have women in tech panels anymore. But I've been reflecting a bit on this lately because I just came from a few years in healthcare, which, from my experience, it's a lot more women in leadership roles. I was a little spoiled, even in our technology organization. And now, I'm back in startups and tech, where the ratios are completely opposite, especially in roles like engineering, which is a team that I run. (00:33:30): And look, this is just, it's math. I think Carta said that 13-something percent of founders last year were women. It's declining year over year. FEMA led founded teams, or at least 2% of venture capital, women hold 30% of senior leadership org roles. Women are 30% of software engineering teams. This is just math. We're just facts. We're not in the room in the equal proportions. And as somebody who has, despite the numbers, had a fairly successful career so far in technology, I feel like I owe it to the industry to say it hasn't been easy and it's still not easy, even at my level. (00:34:09): And what I want to be clear about, because it gets talked about a lot in forms like this, this is not about imposter syndrome. How could I have any right to imposter syndrome? I've proven myself. I've been a founder, I've raised venture capital, I've had a successful exit. I've been, as you said, a CPO across increasing large teams. I get to invest in red companies. I'm on boards. I get to be on this podcast. I'm a TikTok influencer. This is not about feeling like an imposter. It's really about, it is hard and it is different, and the numbers pencil out in a way that is not favorable to women. (00:34:47): And as you said, there's been a lot of stuff in the past that you look at me now and you say, "Oh, she did associate and all the way up," but I had to fight for my all-girls school to carry computer science at the same rate that the all-boys school had it naturally. I grew up in teeny tiny startups in the early aughts. I saw some nonsense. I had VCs tell me, "Don't get pregnant," when I was... These things happened. And yet here I am, and it's fine. (00:35:21): And I'm not complaining. I just think what people also don't understand is that stuff still happens. I don't need to litigate who it happens with, where it happens. It still happens. I have arrived and it still happens. And the reason I bring this up is I think it should be a point of reflection for industry, and I think it can be a really effective point of reflection for women who want to get into leadership roles. (00:35:46): And the way I approach it is I'm just very curious. I wonder what is structural about technology that creates these things happen? What is cultural? What is external? What has happened to me or happens around me? What is internal? What do I bring into the room that doesn't serve me? And so I try to stay very curious. And then constant product thinker, what are the points of leverage I can use to move things not just forward for me, but for the industry broadly? How can I influence thinking? Where can I not? Where can I walk away from things? (00:36:24): And then as for the internal aspect of it, I think this is also a very powerful thing, which is I try to stay in an empowered space. I know my value. I have no time for imposter syndrome. It's not a constructive thing for me, but I do think knowing that, as I said earlier, the universe is bendable to your will. There are things we can change. I don't think these numbers are not tractable. And so my recommendation and what I'd love to say to the industry generally, to women in particular, is curiosity and empowerment have been my path to joy in this sometimes complicated industry. And I think there's a lot better we can do. There's a little bit of ways to go.
turns.zh: 是的，我很高兴谈论这个。我知道很多人不想被定义或不断被问及担任 C 级领导角色的女性或母亲。我们不要再让女性出现在科技小组中了。但我最近对此进行了一些反思，因为我刚刚在医疗保健行业工作了几年，根据我的经验，担任领导职务的女性要多得多。即使在我们的技术组织中，我也有点被宠坏了。现在，我又回到了初创公司和科技公司，两者的比例完全相反，尤其是在我管理的团队中，比如工程部门。 (00:33:30)：看，这就是数学。我记得 Carta 说过，去年 13% 左右的创始人是女性。它正在逐年下降。 FEMA 领导成立的团队，或至少 2% 的风险投资，女性在组织高级领导职位中占 30%。软件工程团队中女性占 30%。这只是数学。我们只是事实。我们在房间里的比例并不相等。尽管数量众多，但作为一个迄今为止在技术领域取得相当成功职业生涯的人，我觉得我应该对这个行业说，这并不容易，而且仍然不容易，即使在我的水平上也是如此。 (00:34:09)：我想澄清的是，因为它以这样的形式被谈论了很多，这与冒名顶替综合症无关。我怎么可能有冒名顶替综合症的权利呢？我已经证明了自己。我曾经是一名创始人，我筹集过风险投资，我也成功退出过。正如您所说，我一直担任越来越多的大型团队的首席产品官。我开始投资红色公司。我在董事会。我要参加这个播客。我是 TikTok 的影响者。这并不是感觉自己像个冒名顶替者。这实际上是因为，这很困难，而且很不同，而且数字以一种不利于女性的方式出现。 (00:34:47)：正如你所说，过去有很多事情，你现在看着我，你会说，“哦，她确实有关联，而且一直在上升，”但我必须为我的女子学校而奋斗，以与男子学校自然拥有的相同速度教授计算机科学。我是在早期的小型初创公司中长大的。我看到了一些废话。当我……这些事情发生时，风险投资家告诉我，“不要怀孕”。但我在这里，这很好。 (00:35:21)：我没有抱怨。我只是认为人们也不明白的是事情仍然会发生。我不需要对这件事发生在谁、发生在哪里进行诉讼。它仍然发生。我已经到了，但这种事仍然发生。我提出这个问题的原因是我认为这应该成为行业的反思点，而且我认为对于想要担任领导角色的女性来说，这可能是一个真正有效的反思点。 (00:35:46)：我处理这个问题的方式是我很好奇。我想知道创造这些事情发生的技术的结构是什么？什么是文化？什么是外在的？我身上发生了什么或者我周围发生了什么？什么是内部？我可以带什么进入不适合我的房间？所以我尽量保持好奇心。然后，作为一名持续的产品思考者，我可以利用哪些杠杆点来推动事情的发展，不仅是为了我自己，也是为了整个行业？我怎样才能影响思维？我哪里不能呢？我可以在哪里远离事物？ (00:36:24)：然后至于它的内部方面，我认为这也是一个非常强大的事情，就是我尝试留在一个被授权的空间中。我知道我的价值。我没有时间去面对冒名顶替综合症。这对我来说不是一件有建设性的事情，但我确实认为知道，正如我之前所说，宇宙是可以屈服于你的意志的。有些事情我们可以改变。我不认为这些数字是不可处理的。因此，我的建议以及我想对整个行业（尤其是女性）说的是，好奇心和赋权是我在这个有时复杂的行业中获得快乐的途径。我认为我们可以做得更好。还有一些路要走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story that you could share if you're comfortable of just something you've gone through or been through that maybe people are like, "Oh, wow, I see what stuff she's dealing with or other women are dealing with that I had no sense of?"
turns.zh: 如果你对自己经历过的事情感到舒服，或者人们可能会说，“哦，哇，我看到她正在处理的事情或其他女人正在处理的事情是我没有意识到的，你可以分享一个故事吗？”

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I've been trying to wrap my head around this one, which is I consistently get asked if I'm technical enough. Not even if I'm technical enough. Let's put enough aside. If I'm technical. And it's fascinating to me because as a technical co-founder of my startup, I wrote code for the first 12 months solo. I led the engineering team there. That code is still in production in very large environments. I have run multi-hundred people, engineering teams for many years, and I spend my Saturdays and Sundays shipping code. This is what I do. And truly, the first question most people ask me is, "Oh, well you're not technical though. You're a product person." (00:38:11): And I've been really trying to unpack where that is coming from. It's hard for me to imagine somebody else that looks different, that has a different name, that has a different gender getting that question with my background. And so that's one of those things that has really been spinning my head. Again, it's not about imposter syndrome. I don't have anything to prove to people, but I am quite curious where that orientation comes from. And if it comes to somebody like me, who has really had some proven success, I know it's happening to other people, and I'm hoping that I can do something from my position to turn that a little bit.
turns.zh: 我一直在努力解决这个问题，即我不断被问到我的技术是否足够。即使我的技术足够好也不行。让我们先把足够的东西放在一边。如果我是技术人员的话。这对我来说很着迷，因为作为我的初创公司的技术联合创始人，我在前 12 个月里独自编写代码。我在那里领导了工程团队。该代码仍在非常大的环境中生产。我多年来一直管理着数百人的工程团队，并且我利用周六和周日的时间来发送代码。这就是我所做的。确实，大多数人问我的第一个问题是，“哦，好吧，你不是技术人员。你是一个产品人员。” (00:38:11)：我一直在努力解开它的来源。我很难想象其他看起来不同、名字不同、性别不同的人会以我的背景来回答这个问题。这就是让我头晕的事情之一。再说一次，这与冒名顶替综合症无关。我没有什么可以向人们证明的，但我很好奇这种取向从何而来。如果它涉及到像我这样确实取得了一些成功的人，我知道这也发生在其他人身上，我希望我能从我的立场做一些事情来扭转这一局面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this connects to what you shared, the advice you had of just try to get curious about why it's happening, which is exactly what you just said. Is that just mostly to help you not get upset and frustrated? Let me just understand, why is this happening again and again?
turns.zh: 这与你分享的内容有关，你的建议是试着好奇为什么会发生这种情况，这正是你刚才所说的。这主要是为了帮助您不感到不安和沮丧吗？让我明白，为什么这样的事一而再再而三地发生？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: One, I do think sitting in your power is very effective. And so curiosity means that I'm in control, and I do think I'm in control more than I'm not. That's one part of it is, I think. And the other thing is I think a lot of this is it's complicated. It's structural, it's cultural. It's what you see and what you don't see, not just in the workplace. It's what you see and don't see in media. Am I reading my 7-year-old and my 4-year-old books of, "My grandma's a software engineer?" (00:39:35): Books called the Mom Test, which I actually think is a great book, but it has this underlying presumption of who is technical, who's not, who understands things, who doesn't. And that all bubbles up into how individuals experience an industry that's driving tremendous economic growth here, where at the end of the day, it's about economic participation. It can be about individuals and aspirations, but it is also about economic participation. (00:40:00): The reason I'm curious about it is I do think it's complicated and I do think you can be successful, but I don't think we're being successful at the rates I would love to see. And I think we're missing a lot of innovation and a lot of economic growth by not having incredible, technical, capable women start companies and lead organizations. And so I think we're all missing out for that, and I'd love to see more of it.
turns.zh: 第一，我确实认为掌握权力非常有效。因此，好奇心意味着我能掌控一切，而且我确实认为我能掌控的程度比我无法掌控的程度要高。我认为这是其中的一部分。另一件事是我认为这很复杂。这是结构性的，也是文化性的。这是你看到的和你没看到的，而不仅仅是在工作场所。这就是你在媒体上看到和看不到的东西。我是在读我 7 岁和 4 岁孩子的书《我的奶奶是一名软件工程师》吗？ (00:39:35)：名为《妈妈测试》的书，我实际上认为这是一本很棒的书，但它有这样一个基本假设：谁是技术人员，谁不是技术人员，谁理解事物，谁不理解事物。这一切都体现在个人如何体验这个推动巨大经济增长的行业，归根结底，这与经济参与有关。它可以与个人和愿望有关，但也与经济参与有关。 (00:40:00)：我对此感到好奇的原因是我确实认为这很复杂，而且我确实认为你可以成功，但我不认为我们会以我希望看到的速度取得成功。我认为，由于没有令人难以置信的、技术精湛、有能力的女性创办公司和领导组织，我们错过了很多创新和大量经济增长。所以我认为我们都错过了这一点，我很想看到更多这样的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is there an answer to how do we do this better? Anything you think, hey, you've seen work to help get us past this?
turns.zh: 我们如何做得更好有答案吗？嘿，你有什么想法可以帮助我们克服这个困难吗？

turns.speaker: Claire Vo
turns.en: I think normalize seeing it, so thanks for bringing me on this podcast, but I do think normalize seeing it is one of the simplest ways. If you close your eyes and imagine a software engineer, my dream is you imagine a diverse set of folks. You don't imagine a very specific art type. And so I do think you can't believe it unless you see it, and so the more that you can provide platforms for diverse voices to talk about their journey in technology, expose that there are leaders out there that come from different backgrounds, technically, culturally, all those things, the more the industry can imagine different types of leaders in different types of roles. (00:41:17): And so I just want to see it more. I want to invest more and raise the voices of female founders. I want to call out their amazing female CTOs out there, all those things. And I think if you can see it, you can start to unlock these very embedded concepts of who is and is not a technology leader who is and is not technical.
turns.zh: 我认为标准化看到它，所以感谢你让我参加这个播客，但我确实认为标准化看到它是最简单的方法之一。如果你闭上眼睛想象一个软件工程师，我的梦想是你想象一群不同的人。你不会想象出一种非常具体的艺术类型。因此，我确实认为，除非亲眼所见，否则你无法相信这一点，因此，你越能为不同的声音提供平台来谈论他们的技术之旅，暴露出来自不同背景、技术、文化等方面的领导者，行业就越能想象不同类型的领导者担任不同类型的角色。 (00:41:17)：所以我只是想看到更多。我想加大投资并提高女性创始人的声音。我想赞扬他们出色的女性首席技术官，诸如此类。我认为，如果你能看到这一点，你就可以开始解开这些非常根深蒂固的概念，即谁是技术领导者，谁不是技术领导者，谁是技术领导者，谁不是技术领导者。

turns.en: Awesome. I love that advice. It's something I try really hard to do with this podcast. (00:41:44): This episode is brought to you by Vanta. Vanta's market-leading trust management platform helps you continuously monitor compliance alongside reporting and tracking risk.
